It helps some tenants in the short run, but it creates broad adverse effects across society. Lower supply, lower mobility, lower housing quality, and so on. But we are here to talk about rent freeze. So here's the flagship study of an actual rent freeze in a major Western city. Forward to the past. Short-term effects of the rent freeze in Berlin by Hahn, Halladielin, Woltl, and Fongoni. Published in 2024 in Management Science. Berlin introduced the Mittendeckel, the rent freeze, in February 2020, freezing rent at June 2019 level. The German Constitutional Court struck it down 13 months later in April 2021. The authors used the difference-in-differences design on real listing data. The key findings? Advertised rent dropped significantly once it was enacted. So the freeze worked in a narrow sense. But there was a sharp reduction in the number of rental listings in Berlin. There was a substitution effect. Rents in Berlin's satellite city Potsdam and adjacent unregulated municipalities rose as landlords and tenants shifted. And three specific mechanisms drove the supply drop. Conversion of rental units into owner-occupied units, a reduction in newly built dwellings, and a drop in properties advertised for rent. The authors' own conclusion was rather pessimistic. Planned rent freezes bring more harm than good. They even included a line in the paper from Swedish economist Asar Lindbeck, who ironically leaned more to the political left, who said, in many cases, rent control appears to be the most efficient technique presently known to destroy a city, except for bombing. So what do I want to say in conclusion? Guys, the laws of economics do not care what you think, what you feel, what you wish would happen, or who you vote for. The same way gravity works the same under monarchy, communism, or capitalism, the patterns of economics tend to hold too. When you artificially put barriers for something, the supply of it tends to go down. Less supply drives up prices and competition. And in that competition, the poor are the ones affected the most, because by default, they can compete less. Those are very simple rules of economics, and they hold whether you like them or not. Simple as that.
